opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think Deep Research is one of those things that really changes how you can learn. If you're someone who's naturally curious, who goes down rabbit holes, the limiting factor has always been time. You'd find a topic you care about and spend hours pulling together sources, reading things that turn out to be irrelevant, trying to synthesize it all yourself.

What's compelling is that you can ask a hard, open-ended question and get back something like a thoughtful report. It's gone out, read a lot, cross-referenced things, and put it together in a way that's useful. That lets you spend your time on the part that's actually fun: thinking about the ideas, asking the next question, pushing deeper.

For me, it's become a way to get up to speed on something quickly and then have a real conversation about it. I'll read the report, find the parts that are most interesting, and follow up. It feels less like searching and more like having a very fast, very diligent research assistant who never gets tired of your questions.

And I think we're still early. As these systems get better at reasoning and at knowing what's reliable, it'll get even more powerful. But even now, for people with an intense appetite for learning, it's a bit of a superpower. It compresses what used to take days into minutes, and that changes how much you can explore.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they read the report, find the most interesting parts, and follow up, describing how the report guides what they ask next.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that's most compelling to me is that it changes what a question can be. For most of my life, if you had a real, deep question about something, you had two options: spend a weekend chasing it down yourself, or find someone who already knew and hope they'd take the time to explain it to you. Most questions never got asked because the cost was too high. You'd just file it away as "huh, I wonder about that" and move on.

Deep Research collapses that cost. You can ask something genuinely hard, something that would take a smart person hours of reading and synthesis, and go do something else, and come back to a thoughtful answer with sources you can check. And what I've noticed, in myself and in other people who use it a lot, is that the number of questions you ask goes way up. The curiosity was always there. It was just being rationed.

The other thing I love is that it's good at the layered question. The first answer leads to a second question, and the second one is better than the first, and you can keep pulling that thread. That's what learning actually feels like when it's going well. It's not reading one summary. It's getting far enough into something that you start to see the shape of what you don't know.

I'll say the part that I find a little humbling too. I used to think of my ability to synthesize a lot of material quickly as a real advantage. It's becoming a commodity. And I think that's great, honestly. It means the scarce thing is taste in what to ask and the willingness to follow it. For people who have that appetite, this is the best time in history to have it.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research’s first answer can lead the user to a better second question, describing how its answers guide continued self-directed inquiry.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that it lets you follow your curiosity much further. You have a question, but getting to a satisfying answer might normally mean hours of finding sources, reading them, and figuring out how they fit together. Deep Research can do a lot of that work and give you something substantial to engage with.

And for someone who loves learning, that answer is usually the beginning. You read it and think, “Wait, why is that true?” or “How does that connect to this other thing?” Then you go deeper. That loop—asking a question, building some understanding, finding a better question—is really exciting to me. You still want to check the evidence and think critically, but you can pursue more of the things you’re curious about.

r001.rationale: The response says a learner reads the answer, develops follow-up questions, and uses them to go deeper, describing reports guiding what they ask next.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that it lets you follow your curiosity much further. You start with a question, but often you don’t know enough yet to ask the really interesting question. You need to understand the landscape, see where people disagree, and figure out what evidence matters.

Deep Research can help you get through that initial work and give you something substantial to engage with. Then you can say, “Wait, that’s surprising. Go deeper on that.” For someone who loves learning, that ability to keep pulling on a thread is really exciting. You still have to think critically and check important claims, but the distance between being curious about something and being able to have an informed conversation about it gets much shorter.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research gives the learner something substantial to engage with, prompting follow-up questions such as “Go deeper on that.”
